record.original_question: A finite set Z in P^n is called geproci if its image under projection from a general point P to a fixed hyperplane H is a complete intersection. In P^3, a set Z is called (a, b)-geproci if its projection is the transverse intersection of curves C_{a,P} and C_{b,P} of degrees a <= b. Find a non-trivial (a, b)-geproci set for which neither C_{a,P} nor C_{b,P} is an unexpected curve, or prove that no such set exists.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{P}^n$ denote projective $n$-space over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$. A finite set $Z \subseteq \mathbb{P}^n$ is said to be geproci (general projection complete intersection) if for a general point $P \in \mathbb{P}^n$, the image $Z_P$ of $Z$ under the linear projection from $P$ onto a fixed hyperplane $H \cong \mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ is a complete intersection in $H$.

Now specialize to $n = 3$. A finite set $Z \subseteq \mathbb{P}^3$ is called $(a,b)$-geproci, with integers $1 \le a \le b$, if for a general $P \in \mathbb{P}^3$ the projection $Z_P \subseteq H$ is the transverse intersection of a plane curve $C_{a,P}$ of degree $a$ and a plane curve $C_{b,P}$ of degree $b$ (so in particular $|Z| = ab$). The set $Z$ is called trivial if it is either a degenerate set (contained in a plane) or a grid (the complete intersection of two unions of skew lines); otherwise $Z$ is non-trivial.

For a finite set $X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^3$ and an integer $d \ge 1$, $X$ is said to admit an unexpected curve of degree $d$ if, denoting by $I(X) \subseteq k[x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3]$ its homogeneous ideal, one has
$$\dim_k [I(X + (d-1)P)]_d \;>\; \max\Bigl\{0,\; \dim_k [I(X)]_d -  inom{d+1}{2}\Bigr\}$$
for a general point $P \in \mathbb{P}^3$, where $(d-1)P$ denotes the $(d-1)$-th symbolic power of the ideal of $P$ (equivalently, $X$ imposes fewer conditions than expected on forms of degree $d$ vanishing to order $d-1$ at a general $P$). For an $(a,b)$-geproci set $Z$, the curves $C_{a,P}$ and $C_{b,P}$ are said to be unexpected (for $Z$) when they arise from such a failure of the expected dimension count.

Problem. Exhibit a non-trivial $(a,b)$-geproci set $Z \subseteq \mathbb{P}^3$ for which neither $C_{a,P}$ nor $C_{b,P}$ is an unexpected curve, or prove that no such set exists.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem appears as an open problem in the recent literature on geproci sets. Surveys and follow-up works from 2022–2024 continue to list the classification of non-trivial geproci sets as largely open, with only a handful of known non-trivial non-half-grid examples (e.g., the $D_4$, $F_4$, $H_4$ configurations) whose associated curves are unexpected. No published resolution of this specific question was found.

status_evidence.title: Geproci sets on skew lines in P^3 with two transversals
status_evidence.snippet: Nontrivial geproci non-half grids are much less well understood; only a few examples are known and all are linked to unexpected curves.
status_evidence.claim: Known non-trivial geproci non-half-grid examples are connected to unexpected curves, leaving the problem of finding one without unexpected curves open.

status_evidence.title: Oberwolfach Report 54/2022
status_evidence.snippet: Open problems concerning the classification and structure of non-trivial geproci sets are discussed.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is listed among open problems on geproci sets.
